The Location Certificate
Introduction

The location certificate is one of the most important — and most misunderstood — documents in a real estate transaction in Quebec. An expired or non-compliant certificate can delay, complicate or derail a sale.
This guide explains what this document is, when it must be renewed, what the irregularities it can reveal are, and how to anticipate it on the seller's side.
Informational content: special cases are handled with the notary and the land surveyor. Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

The location certificate is one of the most misunderstood documents — and one of the most capable of delaying a sale. This guide explains its role, when it must be renewed, the irregularities it reveals, and how to anticipate costs and timelines.
The key message: deal with it early, never the day before signing.
What is a location certificate?
Understanding the role of this survey document.
Understanding the role of this survey document.

The location certificate is a document prepared by a land surveyor that describes the property's current state: lot boundaries, the location of the buildings, easements, any encroachments, and compliance with the regulations and titles.
It includes a plan and a report. It lets the buyer, the lender and the notary know exactly what is being sold and whether everything is compliant.

The location certificate is a survey document that describes the property's condition and situation (boundaries, buildings, easements, encroachments). The lender and the notary require it: it's a key document that must reflect the current reality at the time of the sale.
Emilie's tip
Think of the location certificate as the property's “ID card”. It's what confirms that what you're selling really matches the titles and the regulations.
When do you need a new certificate?
Knowing whether yours is still valid.
Knowing whether yours is still valid.
A certificate can become insufficient if it's too old or no longer reflects the current state of the premises. The notary and the lender require a certificate that matches the present reality.
Too old: standards and the state of the premises may have changed.
Changes since (an addition, a shed, a pool, a fence, a driveway): the certificate doesn't show them.
A regulatory or boundary change: can make it non-compliant.
When in doubt, order a new certificate from a land surveyor. It takes time: better to start early.

A certificate becomes insufficient if it's too old or no longer matches the state of the premises (an addition, a shed, a pool, a fence, a new easement). When in doubt, have it checked early: producing a new certificate takes time you shouldn't discover at the last minute.
Emilie's tip
If you've added anything since your certificate (a shed, a pool, an addition), assume it needs updating. Anticipate: a surveyor doesn't produce a certificate overnight.
The irregularities it can reveal
Anticipating the problems to fix before the sale.
Anticipating the problems to fix before the sale.
Encroachment: a building (yours or a neighbour's) that crosses the boundary.
Easement: a third party's right over your lot (right-of-way, public utility).
Non-compliance with setbacks or municipal regulations.
A discrepancy between the reality and the titles.
Some irregularities are minor; others require fixes, a regularization or a negotiation. Discovering them early keeps them from blocking the sale at the last minute.

The certificate can reveal irregularities to fix: an encroachment (a building that crosses a boundary), non-compliance with the regulations, a forgotten easement. Better to discover them — and deal with them — before the sale than to have them block the transaction at the notary's.
Emilie's tip
Have your certificate read by the notary BEFORE listing. Settling an irregularity upfront is far simpler than discovering it under pressure, an offer in hand.
Costs, timelines and good anticipation
Planning this often-forgotten item.
Planning this often-forgotten item.
A new certificate represents a cost (the surveyor's fees, varying by property) and above all a production lead time. In a sale, that lead time can be critical if you start late.
Check your certificate as soon as you consider selling.
Order a new one early if necessary.
Factor this cost and lead time into your selling schedule.

A new certificate represents a cost (surveyor's fees) and above all a lead time. It's an often-forgotten item: anticipate it from the decision to sell, and negotiate in the promise to purchase who pays for it, to avoid last-minute tensions.
Emilie's tip
Treat the location certificate as the very first box to check in your sale. It's the document that, forgotten, most often delays a signing at the notary's.
